topic: Chemistry — The particulate nature of matter
subject: science

items.q: Why does a solid, such as a block of iron, keep its own shape?
items.correct: Its particles are held in fixed places
items.misconception: Its particles are too hard to bend
items.why: Students explain what they can see (a solid expanding, a gas being squashed, a hard solid) by giving the same property to the particles. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports students who say particles can 'expand, change shape and colour, or shrink' (Happs, 1980), and that about half of 18-year-olds think water molecules in steam are larger than those in ice (Griffiths and Preston, 1992). IOP Spark lists 'Some students think that when air is heated the particles expand and cause high pressure' (Ayas, Özmen and Calik, 2009). Keep two levels apart. Expanding, being squashed and being hard are properties of the whole substance; each particle stays the same size and does not change.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
items.random_wrong: Its particles are not moving at all

items.q: Which describes the particles in liquid water?
items.correct: Touching, random, and sliding past each other
items.misconception: In neat rows, with small gaps between them
items.why: Many diagrams show a liquid as a solid's rows with a few gaps, so students copy that picture. IOP Spark lists 'Some students draw liquid particle diagrams with a regular pattern': 'The patterns may be similar to patterns in solids but with more space between some of the particles' (Adbo and Taber, 2009, International Journal of Science Education). Draw a liquid with the particles touching but jumbled, with no rows. They are about as close together as in the solid; they are not spread out.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
items.random_wrong: Close together, with more water filling the gaps

items.q: The diagram shows the particles of a gas in a sealed jar. Half of the gas is pumped out. How are the remaining particles arranged?
items.correct: Spread out evenly through the whole jar
items.misconception: Packed together at the bottom of the jar
items.why: Solids and liquids settle at the bottom of a container, so students expect gas particles to do the same. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Novick and Nussbaum (1978), who asked 13–14-year-olds to draw the air left in a flask after some was pumped out: 'A significant proportion drew air around the sides of the flask, or in a mass at the bottom.' A gas always fills its whole container. With fewer particles, they are simply further apart.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
items.random_wrong: Gathered near the top, as gas particles float

items.q: What causes the pressure of the air inside a sealed bottle?
items.correct: Air particles hitting all of the walls
items.misconception: Air particles pulling on one another
items.why: Students know that forces hold solids together and carry the idea over to gases. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports that 'a significant proportion of 15-year-olds use attractive forces between gas particles to help explain air pressure' (Brook, Briggs and Driver, 1984), and that 'Some students suggest the strength of the forces is temperature dependent'. In a gas the particles are far apart and the forces between them are tiny. The push on the walls comes from the particles hitting them.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
items.random_wrong: Air particles packed tight against the walls

items.q: The diagram shows gas particles in a sealed metal can. The can is warmed in hot water. Why does the gas pressure rise?
items.correct: The particles hit the walls harder and more often
items.misconception: Particles of heat get in and add to the gas
items.why: Everyday language treats heat and cold as things that move ('shut the door, you're letting the cold in'). Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports secondary students who say 'heat is a substance in its own right', that bubbles in boiling water are made of heat, and that 'coldness comes through the glass' (Osborne and Cosgrove, 1983); IOP Spark lists 'Some students think of cold as an entity that behaves in ways similar to heat'. That a student holding this idea would call the white cloud above a kettle 'heat' is our inference. Talk about energy being transferred. In a freezer, energy is transferred from the water to its colder surroundings; nothing called 'cold' moves in.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
items.random_wrong: The particles get bigger and push on the walls

items.q: Air is sealed in a syringe. The plunger is pushed in and held still for a minute. Why is the air pressure now higher?
items.correct: Its particles hit the walls more often
items.misconception: Its particles are now touching each other
items.why: Diagrams usually fit a gas into a small box, which hides how much empty space there really is. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Benson et al. (1993), in whose study about a third of university science students 'seriously underestimated the relative amount of space between the gas particles themselves'. The step from this to 'packed particles press on the walls' is our inference. Picture a gas as a few particles in a huge, mostly empty space. Even when it is squashed, its particles are still far apart.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
items.random_wrong: Its particles have been squashed smaller

items.q: A sealed syringe of air can be pushed in a long way. The same syringe filled with water hardly moves. Why?
items.correct: Air particles have large spaces between them
items.misconception: Water particles have water in the gaps
items.why: Empty space is hard to imagine, and the things we see seem 'full', so students fill the gaps with air or with the substance. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Novick and Nussbaum (1978), who found that 25% of 13–14-year-olds thought the space between particles was filled, for example with air, dust or other gases; Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC) reports learners who say there is water between the particles of water, or air between the particles. Between particles there is nothing at all. In a gas the empty spaces are large; in solids and liquids the particles touch, so the spaces are tiny.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
items.random_wrong: Air particles are soft and squash easily

items.q: The diagram shows the particles of a substance before and after it melts. What happens to the particles as it melts?
items.correct: They leave fixed places and move around
items.misconception: They melt and turn into tiny drops of liquid
items.why: Students give the particles the change they can see in the substance. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports that 'About half of 15-year-olds think ice particles can shrink, expand, dissolve or melt when changing to liquid water', and gives 15-year-olds' answers in which particles 'melted or died' (Brook, Briggs and Driver, 1984). Solid, liquid and gas describe the substance, not single particles. Only the arrangement and movement of the particles change.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: They dissolve and turn the solid into a solution

items.q: Pure water has been boiling in a beaker for ten minutes. Big bubbles keep forming inside the water. What is in the bubbles?
items.correct: Water that has turned into a gas
items.misconception: Air that was mixed into the water
items.why: Small bubbles of dissolved air really do appear when water is first warmed, and any gas around us gets called 'air'. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Osborne and Cosgrove (1983), in whose study of 8–17-year-olds 'the bubbles were made of heat, air, oxygen or hydrogen and steam'. Once water has boiled for a while, the big bubbles are water vapour: water particles that have broken away from the liquid inside it.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen and oxygen from split water

items.q: A thin layer of water is left on a glass plate. A day later the plate is dry. What happened to the water particles?
items.correct: They escaped from the surface into the air
items.misconception: They only left once the water had boiled
items.why: Students first meet 'liquid to gas' as boiling a kettle, so turning into a gas is linked with boiling. Yalcin (2012, Chemistry Education Research and Practice) lists, from earlier studies of older students, the beliefs 'Heating is necessary for evaporation' (Coştu et al., 2010) and 'Vaporization starts with boiling' (Canpolat et al., 2006); Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports young children who say an outside agent, such as the Sun, makes water evaporate. Evaporating happens at the surface, at temperatures below the boiling point; boiling happens all through the liquid, at the boiling point.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: They were used up and no longer exist

items.q: The diagram shows a can of drink just out of a fridge. Drops of water form on the outside. Where does this water come from?
items.correct: Water vapour in the air that condenses
items.misconception: Drink seeping out through the metal
items.why: The drops appear on the container that holds the drink, so students link the two. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Osborne and Cosgrove (1983), whose pupils aged 8–15 said 'water comes through the glass'. Air always contains some water vapour. When it touches a cold surface it cools and condenses into drops; a cold, empty glass gets wet on the outside too.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: Coldness from the can turning into water

items.q: Water boils in a kettle. Just above the spout is a clear gap, then a white cloud. What is the white cloud?
items.misconception: Water vapour, which is a gas
items.why: In everyday speech the white cloud is called 'steam', and steam is described as water vapour. Yalcin (2012, Chemistry Education Research and Practice) reports Chang (1997), in which 70% of students thought the white smoke from a kettle was water vapour, and Osborne and Cosgrove (1983), whose students called the visible mist 'steam'. Water vapour is invisible. A white cloud or mist is made of tiny drops of liquid water that have condensed from the vapour.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: Heat you can see in the air

items.q: A tray of water is put in a freezer and turns to ice. What happens during freezing?
items.correct: The water transfers energy to its surroundings
items.misconception: All of the particles stop moving completely
items.why: A solid looks completely still, and particle diagrams are still pictures of tightly packed circles, so the particles seem frozen in place. IOP Spark (Institute of Physics) lists 'Many students think that atoms do not move in a solid', citing Andersson (1990, Studies in Science Education), who notes that textbook illustrations can give false impressions about movement. Particles are always moving. In a solid they vibrate on the spot in fixed places; heating makes them vibrate faster.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: Cold flows from the freezer into the water

items.q: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. At room temperature it turns straight into a gas. What happens to its particles?
items.correct: They break free and spread far and wide
items.misconception: They lose their weight and float away
items.why: Gases are invisible, balloons float and 'light as air' is an everyday phrase, so gases seem weightless. IOP Spark lists 'Many students think that gas/air particles float' (Lee and Kwok, 2010, Physics Education); Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports students who think 'gas weighs less than liquid' (Stavy, 1990). That such students would also say air particles are lighter than water particles, or lose weight when they become a gas, is our inference. Every particle has mass. A gas fills its whole container because its particles move quickly in all directions. The particles in air are in fact heavier than water particles.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: They each swell up into bigger particles

items.q: Does a gas that is just sitting still in a closed container press on the walls?
items.correct: Yes. Even when nothing is squashing it, the gas particles are moving fast and hitting the walls all the time, so the gas presses on every wall.
items.misconception: A gas only presses on its container while it is being squashed or is moving; still air does not push on anything.
items.why: We only notice air pushing when we squeeze it or when it moves as wind, so still air seems to do nothing. IOP Spark lists 'Many students think that static gas does not apply pressure', explaining that 'students may think that gas can only exert pressure when being actively compressed' (Andersson, 1990, pupils aged 12–16). The particles of a still gas are moving and hitting the walls all the time. Squashing a gas does not start its pressure; it makes the hits more frequent.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is melting the same as dissolving?
items.correct: No. Melting is one substance changing from solid to liquid when energy is transferred to it. Dissolving is a solid mixing into a liquid (such as sugar into water) to make a solution.
items.misconception: Melting and dissolving are the same thing: when a solid melts it 'dissolves' and becomes a solution.
items.why: In everyday speech sugar 'melts' in tea, and both changes leave a liquid. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports that 'Melting and dissolving are used frequently as synonyms', and gives 15-year-olds' answers that melting particles 'turn from a crystal form to a solution form' (Brook, Briggs and Driver, 1984). Melting involves one substance and heating. Dissolving involves two substances: a solid (the solute) and a liquid (the solvent).
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: When water boils or evaporates, does it split into hydrogen and oxygen?
items.correct: No. Boiling and evaporating are changes of state, not chemical reactions. The water particles stay as water particles: no hydrogen or oxygen is made, and none joins up to make water when it condenses.
items.misconception: Turning water into a gas splits it into hydrogen and oxygen, and these gases join up again to make water when it condenses.
items.why: Students learn that water contains hydrogen and oxygen, and that air contains oxygen, so they use those names for the gas. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Osborne and Cosgrove (1983), whose students said the bubbles in boiling water were oxygen or hydrogen and that, in condensation, oxygen and hydrogen recombine to form water; IOP Spark lists 'Some students think that oxygen and hydrogen condense together to form water droplets'. In every change of state the particles stay the same. Water vapour is made of water particles; when it cools, they come together again as liquid water.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: When water evaporates, or dry ice turns to gas, do the particles stop existing?
items.correct: No. The particles are not destroyed. They move into the air as a gas, where they are spread out and too small to see.
items.misconception: When a liquid evaporates (or a solid turns into a gas), some or all of the substance is used up or disappears: its particles no longer exist.
items.why: A dried-up puddle or a vanished lump of dry ice seems simply gone, because the gas cannot be seen. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports young children saying that evaporated water has 'disappeared' (Russell et al., 1989), and Stavy's finding that '50% of 15 year olds do not conserve the amount of matter in evaporation'. Applying the idea to dry ice is our inference. Particles are never destroyed in a change of state. The mass of the gas formed equals the mass of the liquid or solid that changed.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: When water left on a plate dries up, has it soaked into the plate?
items.correct: No. A glass or glazed plate does not soak up water. The water particles escaped from the surface of the water into the air: the water evaporated.
items.misconception: Water that dries up from a surface has soaked into the thing it was on (the plate, the table or the floor).
items.why: Water does soak into paper, cloth and soil, so students extend that to every surface. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Cosgrove and Osborne (1981), whose pupils said the water 'went into the plate' when it was left to evaporate. On a surface that cannot soak it up, drying is evaporation: the particles leave the surface of the water and go into the air.
items.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
